chapter.title: Reading a real one, start to finish

cards.body: The most useful column on a balance sheet is the one almost everyone skips: last year's. Reading a real balance sheet is like inspecting a house you might buy. You walk the same route every time, front door to attic, holding last year's photo of the same house, because **cracks only show up when you compare**.
cards.simpler: Most people skip last year's column on a balance sheet, but it is the most useful one. Reading a real balance sheet is like looking over a house you might buy. You take the same path each time, from the front door up to the attic, with last year's photo of the same house in your hand, because **cracks only show up when you compare**.

cards.prompt: You're touring a flat you might buy. The agent swears the ceiling is fine. What tells you most about that brown patch above the sofa?

options.text: A sharp photo of the ceiling, taken this morning
This morning's photo next to one from last spring, when the patch was half the size
The agent's written description, which calls it character

whyNot.a: That's size, not direction: one photo shows how big the patch is, not whether it's growing.
whyNot.c: That's the sales pitch, not the evidence: you want something you can check yourself.

cards.reteach: One picture tells you how big something is. Two pictures a year apart tell you which way it's heading and how fast. A balance sheet prints both, this year's column and last year's, side by side.

cards.title: The route, part one
cards.body:
Start at the very top. Find the company name, the date of the photo, and the unit. The unit hides in small print, *in thousands* or *in millions*. Miss it and every number is off by a factor of 1,000.

Next, find the three totals: total assets, total liabilities, total equity. Check that the first equals the other two added together. That takes 30 seconds.

Then walk the rooms in order: current assets, long-term assets, current liabilities, long-term debt, equity. **Same order, every time**, the way a good inspector always checks the boiler before the bedrooms, so nothing gets missed.
cards.simpler: Start at the top. Find the company name, the date, and the unit, which hides in small print as *in thousands* or *in millions*. Miss it and every number is off by 1,000 times. Next, find total assets, total liabilities and total equity, and check that the first equals the other two added. That takes 30 seconds. Then read each section in order: current assets, long-term assets, current liabilities, long-term debt, equity. **Same order, every time**, so nothing gets missed.

cards.title: Linden Cycles has a record year
cards.body: Say you open the report of a bike maker, call it Linden Cycles, dated 31 December, in thousands. The totals match: 4,800 owned, 3,000 owed, 1,800 left for the owners. Now read across to last year: cash fell from 900 to 300, unpaid customer bills doubled from 700 to 1,400, and bills due within 12 months rose from 1,100 to 1,600. Profit was 400, yet cash dropped 600, so all three warning signs are on one page. Page one of the same report calls it *a record year*.
cards.simpler: Picture a bike maker called Linden Cycles. Its report is dated 31 December, in thousands. The totals match: 4,800 owned, 3,000 owed, 1,800 left for the owners. Now compare with last year. Cash fell from 900 to 300. Unpaid customer bills doubled from 700 to 1,400. Bills due within 12 months rose from 1,100 to 1,600. Profit was 400, yet cash dropped 600. **All three warning signs are on one page**, while the first page calls it *a record year*.

cards.prompt: Mill Street Bakery, in thousands. Cash: 120 last year, 110 now. Unpaid customer bills: 80 last year, 240 now. Bills due this year: 150 last year, 160 now. Which line do you flag first?

options.text: Unpaid customer bills, because they tripled
Bills due this year, because they went up

whyNot.a: That's a small dip, not a warning: 10 out of 120 is less than a tenth.
whyNot.c: That's normal drift, not a jump: 150 to 160 is a rise of under 7%.

cards.reteach: Don't ask which number is biggest or which one went down. Ask which line changed most compared with its own old number. Customers owing three times as much means the bakery is handing out bread and waiting to be paid.

cards.title: The cupboards: notes and odd names
cards.body:
Once a line jumps, open the cupboard. Most lines carry a small number pointing to a *note* at the back of the report: a page explaining what sits inside that line. The jump is the stain on the ceiling; the note is the pipe above it.

Some names look odd. *Goodwill* is the extra a company paid for another business, above the value of its parts. *Right-of-use assets* are buildings or machines it leases rather than owns.

Benjamin Graham and Spencer Meredith wrote a whole book that reads each line in plain words. For now, **you only need the notes behind the lines that moved**.
cards.simpler: When a line jumps, find its *note*: the small number beside it points to a page at the back explaining what is inside. The jump is the stain on the ceiling; the note is the pipe above it. *Goodwill* is the extra paid for another business, above its parts' value. *Right-of-use assets* are buildings or machines rented, not owned. Graham and Meredith wrote a book on every line. For now, **you only need the notes behind the lines that moved**.

cards.body: Sam opens a balance sheet, checks that assets equal liabilities plus equity to the last dollar, and writes *healthy* in the margin. You'd think a sheet that balances is in good shape. But every balance sheet balances, failing ones too; that proves the arithmetic, not the business. How to spot it: **if you decided before reading last year's column, you haven't read the sheet yet**.
cards.simpler: Sam opens a balance sheet, checks that assets equal liabilities plus equity to the last dollar, and writes *healthy* in the margin. It feels like a sheet that balances must be fine. But every balance sheet balances, even for failing companies. Balancing only proves the sums add up, not that the business is doing well. Here is the test: **if you decided before reading last year's column, you haven't read the sheet yet**.

cards.prompt: You have five minutes with a real balance sheet. Where is a warning sign most likely to show itself?

options.text: In the line where total assets equal liabilities plus equity
In the gap between this year's and last year's number on the same line
In the date printed at the top

whyNot.a: That's the equation, not a warning: it matches on every sheet, healthy or failing.
whyNot.c: That's the label on the photo, not the house: it tells you which day, not what's wrong.

cards.reteach: The equation always holds, and the date only names the day. Trouble shows up as movement: cash shrinking, customer debts swelling, short-term bills climbing. You only see movement when two years sit side by side.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Read a balance sheet the same way every time: date and units, the three totals, then each line next to last year's. **The warning signs are the lines that moved most**, and the notes tell you why.

Next: two full years side by side, and the story of what changed.
cards.simpler: Read a balance sheet the same way every time. First the date and units, then the three totals, then each line next to last year's. **The warning signs are the lines that moved most**, and the notes explain why. Next comes two full years side by side, and the story of what changed.

cards.body: Search for a listed company you know plus *annual report balance sheet*. Find the unit, check the three totals, then circle the one current line that moved most since last year.
cards.simpler: Pick a company you know whose shares trade on the stock market. Search for its name plus *annual report balance sheet*. Open it and find the unit first. Then check that the three totals add up. Finally, circle the **one current line that moved most** since last year, where current means due or used up within a year.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now read a real published balance sheet start to finish, compare each line with last year's, and say whether anything worries you.
